newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel rejects Medicaid kid's health plan.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel rejects Medicaid kid's health plan.

text.p: Ignoring a personal plea from President Clinton, a Senate committee Tuesday rejected a plan to deliver health care to uninsured children through Medicaid, calling instead for broad block grants to states.

The 11-9 defeat came after heavy lobbying from Republican leaders and state governors, who said they should be given broad latitude to design their own programs to cover up to half the nation's 10 million uninsured children.
After hours of private meetings and repeated phone calls from governors, four supporters of the Medicaid proposal, including three Democrats, changed position and voted nay.

"(Opponents) are concerned that we might have 50 different plans," said Texas Republican Sen. Phil Gramm, who called Medicaid expansion too bureaucratic and expensive. "(I) rejoice that we might have 50 different plans because states can learn from each other."

Supporters of the Medicaid plan, offered by Rhode Island Republican John Chafee and West Virginia Democrat Jay Rockefeller, argued that block grants were too broad and would not ensure consistent, comprehensive health care to children.
They said the most cost-effective approach was to use the existing Medicaid program for the poor, elderly and disabled, which covers 25 percent of children under age 18.
"Instead of getting additional children what we will find is states take the money and fund other programs not related to children," said North Dakota Democrat Kent Conrad.
The panel later blocked an effort by Utah Republcan Orrin Hatch to increase the federal cigarette tax to further expand children's care.

The action came as the Finance Committee began debate on massive budget legislation that included $115 billion in five-year Medicare cuts, a $13.6 billion Medicaid reduction to children's health and new welfare initiatives.
The $16 billion children's health plan is one of the only major new domestic initiatives in a five-year budget deal worked out between Congress and the White House.

While there is broad support in Congress for expanding health coverage to children, crafting legislation to implement the budget has opened fault lines between Congress and the White House and within the two political parties.

A House committee has already passed its version of the children's health bill, providing block grants to states. The White House has warned that approach would not result in meaningful coverage because states could use the new money to replace existing services.
Apparently believing Chafee had the votes, Clinton earlier Tuesday went out of his way to endorse his Medicaid plan.
"This (compromise) legislation would be the biggest investment in children's health care since Medicaid passed in 1965," Clinton said at the White House.
"It would be the most significant thing that we could do ... by committing us to providing health insurance coverage to up to five million uninsured children," he said.
The defeat is the latest in a series of setbacks for Clinton, who has accused Republicans of reneging on tax, welfare and other budget agreements.
But governors argued the Chafee plan, which called for $12 billion in Medicaid expansion and $4 billion in new state grants was too expensive.
While the program would have been voluntary, states would have been required to first expand their existing Medicaid programs to access the new funds.

Governors' aides pointed to a Congressional Budget Office estimate that due to the expense, few states would have met a requirement in the plan to keep poor children on the Medicaid rolls for a full year at a time.
The legislation crafted by Finance Committee Chairman William Roth would take the $16 billion and give states the option of choosing a block grant or expansion of the Medicaid program.

Under last minute changes to the plan, states would have to agree to cover poor children up to age 19 under medicaid to get block grant money. They would have to put up some of their own funds and would also have to use the block grant money for insurance policies comparable to those offered federal employees.
Opponents pointed out those insurance policies could have high deductibles and did not provide the broad array of preventive services offered under Medicaid.
The White House in a letter said Roth's plan was written in such a way that "given the incentives ... no rational state would choose Medicaid."
